### Freddie Mac Mortgage Probability of Default {#sec-freddie-mac}

The second empirical study applies the same model set to a structurally different credit problem: residential mortgage probability of default. The data are drawn from the Freddie Mac Single-Family Loan-Level Dataset, a publicly available supervisory-quality source covering origination characteristics and monthly loan performance for conforming mortgages purchased or guaranteed by Freddie Mac. This dataset is widely used in mortgage credit-risk research and regulatory stress-testing [@basel_committee_basel_2011] because it provides the granularity needed for loan-level PD modelling: origination credit score (FICO), combined loan-to-value (CLTV), debt-to-income ratio (DTI), original unpaid principal balance (UPB), coupon rate, loan purpose, property type, occupancy status, geographic region, and origination vintage.

The mortgage setting differs from the credit-card benchmark of @sec-credit-card in three material respects. First, the default rate is far lower: approximately 1.7% versus 22.1%, making this a heavily imbalanced classification problem where the positive class is rare and most conventional threshold-dependent metrics become uninformative at any fixed cutoff. Second, the feature space includes structured domain covariates (FICO, LTV, DTI, vintage era, refinancing incentive) whose interactions are well-studied in the mortgage finance literature and carry direct economic interpretation. Third, the regulatory context is more demanding: mortgage PD models feed directly into Basel IRB capital calculations, IFRS 9 expected credit loss provisions, and CCAR/DFAST stress-testing submissions, where probability calibration is subject to direct supervisory scrutiny [@eba_gl_2017_16; @iasb_ifrs9_2014; @federal_reserve_sr11_7].

#### Data Preparation and Experimental Design {#sec-fm-data}

Origination and monthly performance files were loaded for all available quarters, retaining only those with at least 24 months of seasoning — the standard observation window for through-the-cycle PD estimation under Basel III [@basel_committee_basel_2011]. A loan is labelled as defaulted if it reached 90+ days past due or experienced a credit-event liquidation (foreclosure, short sale, or related disposition) within 24 months of origination. This definition aligns with the Basel IRB default definition and is standard across the mortgage PD literature.

From the pool of qualifying origination records, a stratified subsample of 30,000 loans was drawn using proportional allocation across three stratification variables: vintage era (pre-crisis, crisis, post-crisis, COVID), refinancing incentive bucket (in-the-money, at-the-money, out-of-the-money based on rate spread relative to cohort median), and US Census geographic region (Northeast, Midwest, South, West). This stratified sampling preserves the portfolio-level distributional structure that drives mortgage default heterogeneity while reducing the dataset to a computationally manageable size.

Pre-processing followed the same conventions as @sec-credit-card. Categorical variables — loan purpose, property type, occupancy status, origination channel, first-time buyer flag, vintage era, refinancing bucket, LTV bucket, and geographic region — were one-hot encoded with `drop_first=True` to avoid the dummy-variable trap. Numeric covariates (credit score, original LTV, DTI, coupon rate, UPB, mortgage insurance percentage, rate spread, number of borrowers, number of units, original term, and origination year) were log-transformed where appropriate and standardised to zero mean and unit variance. The scaler was fit on training data only to prevent leakage.

The 30,000-loan sample was split into a fixed held-out test set of 6,000 observations (20%), stratified by the target. The remaining 24,000 observations form the development pool. Three training-set size tiers were evaluated:

- **Small** ($N_{\text{dev}} = 500$): 425 training, 75 validation observations.
- **Medium** ($N_{\text{dev}} = 5{,}000$): 4,250 training, 750 validation observations.
- **Large** ($N_{\text{dev}} = 24{,}000$): 20,400 training, 3,600 validation observations (full development set).

The test set default rate is 1.73% across all tiers — approximately one-thirteenth the rate observed in the credit-card benchmark. This extreme class imbalance means that a naive majority-class classifier achieves 98.3% accuracy, rendering accuracy-based evaluation meaningless. The analysis therefore focuses on ROC-AUC for discrimination and ECE for calibration.

#### Model Set and Training Configuration {#sec-fm-models}

The model set is identical to @sec-uci-models: logistic regression (`class_weight="balanced"`), random forest (500 trees, `class_weight="balanced_subsample"`), XGBoost (`scale_pos_weight`, early stopping on validation), SVGP (512 inducing points, 150 epochs), DSVGP-2L (128 inducing points per layer, hidden dimension 5), and DSVGP-3L.

The low default rate creates a specific challenge for threshold selection. At 1.73% base rate, a well-calibrated model should output probabilities near 0.017 for the majority of observations. The sigmoid-linked GP posterior naturally produces such concentrated estimates, meaning the predicted probability mass lies far below the conventional $0.5$ threshold. At $t = 0.5$, F1 is exactly zero for random forest, SVGP, DSVGP-2L, and DSVGP-3L across all tiers — these models correctly assign very low default probabilities to the overwhelmingly non-default majority, resulting in zero positive predictions at that cutoff. This makes using a fixed $0.5$ threshold absurd for this dataset; even well-calibrated models that perfectly track the true 1.7% default rate would appear to "fail" at this cutoff. All threshold-dependent metrics below are therefore reported at each model's **F1-optimal threshold** ($t^*$), which ranges from 0.02 to 0.81 depending on model and tier. Even at optimal thresholds, the best achievable F1 is approximately 0.15, reflecting the fundamental difficulty of achieving high precision and recall simultaneously at 1.73% prevalence. ROC-AUC, which evaluates the full ranking over all thresholds, is the appropriate primary metric. Statistical uncertainty in all metrics is quantified via 2,000-resample bootstrap confidence intervals (percentile method); see @sec-appendix-ci.

#### Results at Full Scale (Large Tier) {#sec-fm-large}

| Model | ROC-AUC | Avg Prec | F1 ($t^*$) | $t^*$ | ECE | Brier | Log Loss | Time (s) |
|:------|:-------:|:--------:|:----------:|:-----:|:---:|:-----:|:--------:|:--------:|
| Logistic Regression | 0.820 | 0.081 | **0.153** | 0.81 | 0.337 | 0.186 | 0.545 | 0.06 |
| Random Forest | 0.774 | 0.062 | 0.143 | 0.24 | 0.055 | 0.023 | 0.114 | 2.36 |
| XGBoost | 0.785 | 0.059 | 0.128 | 0.59 | 0.400 | 0.184 | 0.555 | 0.20 |
| SVGP | 0.819 | 0.079 | 0.141 | 0.07 | 0.003 | **0.017** | **0.076** | 148.7 |
| DSVGP-2L | 0.821 | **0.084** | 0.137 | 0.09 | **0.002** | **0.016** | **0.075** | 167.8 |
| DSVGP-3L | **0.823** | 0.082 | 0.137 | 0.07 | 0.004 | **0.016** | **0.076** | 650.2 |

: Principal six-model comparison at full scale ($N_{\text{train}} = 20{,}400$, $N_{\text{test}} = 6{,}000$). All threshold-dependent metrics reported at each model's F1-optimal threshold $t^*$. Bold entries indicate leading values. {#tbl-fm-large}

The most striking feature of @tbl-fm-large is the enormous variation in optimal thresholds: GP models require $t^* \in [0.07, 0.09]$ while logistic regression requires $t^* = 0.81$ and XGBoost requires $t^* = 0.59$. This divergence arises because well-calibrated models (the GP family) produce predicted probabilities clustered near the true base rate of 1.7%, while miscalibrated models (logistic regression, XGBoost) produce inflated probability estimates that must be thresholded much higher to separate defaults from non-defaults.

![ROC and precision-recall curves at full scale. DGP models lead on ROC-AUC (0.821–0.823); logistic regression matches the single-layer SVGP at 0.819–0.820.](/sections/4-modeling/assets/freddie-mac/large/roc_pr.png){#fig-fm-large-roc-pr}

![Reliability diagrams at full scale. GP-family models track the diagonal closely (ECE $\leq 0.004$); logistic regression (ECE = 0.337) and XGBoost (ECE = 0.400) show critical miscalibration.](/sections/4-modeling/assets/freddie-mac/large/calibration.png){#fig-fm-large-calibration}

DGP models lead on ROC-AUC point estimates (DSVGP-3L = 0.823, DSVGP-2L = 0.821) but with only $\approx 104$ positives in the test set, bootstrap 95% CIs span $\pm 0.04$ and **no pairwise differences are statistically significant** (@sec-appendix-ci). The tentative GP advantage over tree ensembles (0.819–0.823 vs 0.774–0.785) is consistent with kernel models better capturing smooth FICO/LTV/DTI relationships [@rasmussen_gaussian_2008].

The calibration advantage is dramatically amplified at this low base rate. GP models achieve ECE = 0.002–0.004 — effectively perfect — while XGBoost (ECE = 0.400) and logistic regression (ECE = 0.337) are severely miscalibrated. The GP family achieves approximately **100$\times$ lower ECE** than XGBoost and Brier/log loss approximately $7\times$ lower, confirming that the Bayesian posterior's benefit is proportionally greater when the true event rate is far from 0.5 [@niculescu_mizil_predicting_2005]. Under Basel IRB, GP-produced PD estimates are directly usable for capital calculation without post-hoc calibration [@eba_gl_2017_16; @iasb_ifrs9_2014].

|:------|:-------------:|:--------------:|:--------------:|
| Logistic Regression | 0.098 (0.61) | 0.112 (0.73) | **0.153** (0.81) |
| Random Forest | 0.088 (0.18) | 0.117 (0.21) | 0.143 (0.24) |

: F1 at optimal threshold $t^*$ (shown in parentheses) across training tiers. The extremely low optimal thresholds for GP models (0.02–0.09) versus classical models (0.18–0.81) reflect the GP family's well-calibrated predictions concentrated near the true 1.73% base rate. {#tbl-fm-f1-scaling}

ROC and precision-recall curves and reliability diagrams at each training tier are provided in @sec-appendix-fm-scaling.

SVGP dominates at small scale (ROC-AUC = 0.764), outperforming all other models by a wide margin — the kernel's inductive bias provides a strong prior for the smooth mortgage risk surface even with limited data. DGP architectures are data-hungry: DSVGP-2L surges from 0.692 (small) to 0.821 (large), the largest absolute gain across both datasets, while DSVGP-3L again collapses at small scale (0.510) before recovering at medium/large [@duvenaud_avoiding_2014].

GP models achieve near-perfect calibration at all scales (ECE $\leq 0.008$ from 425 training observations), while classical calibration is unstable — XGBoost ECE fluctuates between 0.180 and 0.400, and logistic regression worsens from 0.118 to 0.337 with more data.

#### Computational Profile {#sec-fm-cost}

![Training time versus ECE for the six models at large scale. GP-family models occupy the lower-right quadrant: higher training cost but dramatically better calibration.](/sections/4-modeling/assets/freddie-mac/large/runtime.png){#fig-fm-runtime width=70%}

| Model | Time (s, small) | Time (s, medium) | Time (s, large) |
|:------|:-------:|:-------:|:-------:|
| Logistic Regression | 0.08 | 0.01 | 0.06 |
| Random Forest | 0.45 | 0.81 | 2.36 |
| XGBoost | 0.03 | 0.10 | 0.20 |
| SVGP | 3.53 | 33.4 | 148.7 |
| DSVGP-2L | 3.59 | 37.1 | 167.8 |
| DSVGP-3L | 12.9 | 136.5 | 650.2 |

: Training time scaling across tiers. Scaling patterns are consistent with the credit-card dataset; DSVGP-3L is approximately $3.9\times$ the cost of DSVGP-2L. {#tbl-fm-runtime}

The computational profile mirrors the credit-card findings. DSVGP-3L at 650.2 s is the most expensive model, approximately $3.9\times$ the cost of DSVGP-2L (167.8 s), yet its ROC-AUC advantage over DSVGP-2L is only +0.002 (0.823 vs 0.821) and its ECE is slightly worse (0.004 vs 0.002). SVGP provides the best cost-effectiveness among GP models: at 148.7 s it delivers ROC-AUC = 0.819 and ECE = 0.003, within 0.004 ROC-AUC of the best model at less than one-quarter the training cost of DSVGP-3L.

#### Summary {#sec-fm-discussion}

The mortgage dataset amplifies the patterns observed on the credit-card benchmark. GP models match or lead on discrimination (ROC-AUC = 0.819–0.823 vs 0.774–0.785 for tree ensembles, though no differences are statistically significant) and deliver **100$\times$ better calibration** than XGBoost (ECE = 0.002–0.004 vs 0.400). At a 1.73% base rate, the Bayesian posterior's benefit is proportionally greater than at 22.1% — the calibration advantage grows from 5–13$\times$ (credit card) to 100–170$\times$ (mortgage), confirming that **the lower the default rate, the greater the relative advantage of GP models for regulatory PD estimation**.

SVGP is the most data-efficient GP variant, leading at small scale (ROC-AUC = 0.764 vs 0.692 for DSVGP-2L). As with the credit-card dataset, the DGP's compositional flexibility does not translate into meaningful performance gains on this smooth risk surface — consistent with the Kin8nm findings (@sec-kin8nm) that depth only helps when the target function has genuinely non-stationary structure.
